Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
News reports about events similar to what happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of witnessed other trauma, the appraisal that others can see what happened to me by looking at me is hard to reconcile unless there was also direct victimization or visible injury. The rest of the profile centers on witnessing, guilt about failing to protect, and anger that perpetrators were not held accountable, which fits. This item implies a conspicuous personal mark or shame signal not otherwise supported by the triggers, memory, or strategies, so it is clinically incoherent within this profile.

vignette: María, a 70-year-old Latin American woman and accomplished fashion designer, has been struggling with intense distress since witnessing her close friend’s traumatic experience during an act of violence. The memory continues to haunt her, especially when she encounters specific triggers that bring the incident back into sharp focus. One cold winter evening, María felt a sudden chill on her skin that instantly transported her back to that fateful day. The tactile sensation triggered an overwhelming reliving of the event, complete with vivid sensory details. This unwelcome intrusion forced its way into her mind when she was least prepared, leaving her disoriented and distressed. She found herself feeling particularly vulnerable in her home studio where she worked late hours, as any slight temperature change could plunge her back into that terrifying moment. The memory’s uncontrolled access and the intensity of her sensory reliving have made it impossible for María to separate her present from the past. Any news report or media coverage related to similar incidents instantly brings back the full force of the trauma. She avoids all news channels and any reminders of the event, pushing away positive emotions because they feel unsafe in this context. The memory is triggered without warning by seemingly mundane things in her surroundings, leaving her feeling powerless. The incident has left María with deep-seated negative appraisals that she cannot shake off. She believes that the people responsible for the violence have faced no consequences, and this lack of accountability adds to her sense of injustice and unresolved trauma. Her self-blame is intense; she feels responsible because she thinks she should have protected her friend but failed in doing so. This belief has led María to adopt maladaptive strategies such as avoiding grief reminders and news reports about similar events. The cycle of her negative appraisals intensifies the memory’s impact, making it more intrusive and vivid. The more she blames herself for failing to protect her friend, the more real the traumatic memory feels. Her self-blame also triggers additional fear responses, where even minor temperature changes on her skin can bring back the full intensity of the memory. Her avoidance behaviors have become habitual over time. María avoids going out when it’s cold and has stopped watching television altogether, fearing that a news report could trigger another episode. The isolation has strained her relationships; she feels increasingly distant from her husband, who is concerned but struggles to understand the depth of her fear. María had come to believe that if she were more alert or acted differently on that day, the outcome might have been different. This belief exacerbates her anxiety and leads her to avoid situations where she may feel a loss of control or face reminders of her friend’s trauma. The memory often forces its way into her mind when she least expects it, causing her to push away positive emotions because they seem unsafe amidst such turmoil. The distress has become so overwhelming that María has finally decided to seek help. She is most afraid of feeling powerless and being unable to protect those around her again. Yet, she also hopes for a chance to find peace, to break the cycle of fear and self-blame that has consumed her life. Despite her deep-seated fears, she recognizes that without intervention, these negative patterns will continue to control her daily existence. María’s journey towards healing is fraught with these interconnected struggles, but her determination to reclaim her sense of safety and well-being remains a beacon of hope in the midst of her trauma.
